source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd
finding: A crowd of 12 different LLMs, aggregated by the median, forecast as well as a crowd of human forecasters. This is the first clean LLM replication of the crowd effect.
numbers: Study 1: 12 LLMs, 31 binary questions, vs 925 human forecasters. Mean Brier: LLM crowd 0.20 (SD 0.12), human crowd 0.19 (SD 0.19), t(60)=0.19, p=0.850. Equivalence test at Cohen d=0.5 (a 0.081 Brier band) passed. No-information benchmark is 0.25.
limits: Only 31 questions. Equivalence test was not preregistered. Models were of different families, so this is a diverse crowd, not one model sampled 12 times. Training-data contamination is possible (see Douven).
agent_relevance: A crowd of mixed models can match a human crowd. The condition that held is model diversity. It is not support for sampling one model many times (G4).

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd (acquiescence)
finding: The LLM crowd had a shared bias: mean predictions sat above 50% although outcomes were almost evenly split. Averaging does not remove a bias all voters share.
numbers: Mean model forecasts significantly above 50% (abstract) with an almost even split of yes/no resolutions.
limits: Single question set. Bias direction may differ by prompt.
agent_relevance: This is the shared-error failure of the crowd idea: the mean inherits common bias. A vote cannot fix what every voter shares, so we need a code check, not more voters.

source: Schoenegger, Tuminauskaite, Park, Tetlock (2024) Wisdom of the Silicon Crowd (Study 2, human median as input)
finding: Showing a model the human crowd median made its forecast better, but a plain average of human and machine was better still.
numbers: GPT-4 Brier 0.17 (SD 0.13) to 0.14 (SD 0.11), p=0.003. Claude 2 0.22 (SD 0.19) to 0.15 (SD 0.14), p<0.001. 186 primary and 186 updated forecasts. Interval width GPT-4 17.75 to 14.22; Claude 2 11.67 to 8.28. Update size correlated with distance from the human median: r=0.88 (GPT-4), r=0.87 (Claude 2). Accuracy gain 17 to 28 percent (abstract).
limits: Models move toward a shown number in proportion to distance, which is anchoring; it helped here only because the shown number was good.
agent_relevance: Models shift toward a displayed answer (matches G5: judges must not see a majority or proposed answer). Combining outside estimates by code beats letting the model absorb them.

source: Douven (2026) Wisdom of LLM Crowds: Aggregation and Contamination in Language Model Ensembles
finding: 15 LLMs on 254 binary prediction-market questions. Learned aggregators (logistic regression, small neural net) beat every single model and all classical aggregators.
numbers: 15 LLMs, 254 questions (208-item set, 94-item clean subset after all training cutoffs). Logistic regression mean Brier reduction 23% vs MLP 15.6%. Best single model on the 208 set: Claude Sonnet 4.6, Brier 0.273.
limits: Learned aggregators are trained on labelled data, which an agent facing one new problem does not have. Small question set.
agent_relevance: Weights learned on past outcomes beat equal votes. If we hold a record of which sampler is right when, use it; otherwise equal-weight votes are weak.

source: Douven (2026) Wisdom of LLM Crowds: Aggregation and Contamination in Language Model Ensembles (contamination)
finding: Much of the apparent gap between big cloud models and small local models was training-data leakage. On questions resolved after every cutoff, the gap nearly vanished.
numbers: Cloud-vs-local gap under arithmetic mean: 35.8% on the full 208 items (Brier 0.254 vs 0.345) to 8.9% on the 94-item clean subset (0.312 vs 0.340). On a nested 48-item subset about 13.4%. Even at each model's own cutoff, LLMs stayed less accurate than the market.
limits: Authors say rankings of individual models were only moderately stable.
agent_relevance: Crowd-wisdom claims on LLMs must be tested on items the models could not have seen. Same lesson as G3: a pass must be on something the answer was not fitted to.

source: Douven (2026) Wisdom of LLM Crowds: Aggregation and Contamination in Language Model Ensembles (disagreement signal)
finding: A symbolic-regression fit to the neural aggregator recovered a pure model-disagreement term as the simplest useful formula. Logistic regression matched the net, so the gain is a linear mix of diverse outputs, not nonlinear tricks.
numbers: Logistic regression comparable to MLP on Brier, accuracy and AUC (abstract and results).
limits: Probability-forecast setting only.
agent_relevance: Spread between independent voters is itself information. That supports using disagreement as the signal that triggers a check (G1) rather than as a vote count.

source: Chetlapalli, Liao, Chen, Chen (2026) Diverse by Reasoning: Harnessing the Wisdom of LLM Crowds for Future Prediction
finding: Among 25 LLMs, a crowd of 3 models (one medoid per behavioural cluster, K-means++) beat plain majority voting over all 25 on both future-prediction benchmarks. Composition mattered more than size.
numbers: 25 LLMs, 350 questions over 2 benchmarks (FutureX-Past, Bench to the Future). Model calls cut 88%, cost cut about 80%. Clusters of 12, 8 and 5 models. Behaviour was measured from reasoning traces on separate development tasks, not from vendor name.
limits: Cost analysis used 100 questions per benchmark. The gain depends on the K-means++ partition: with hierarchical clustering the medoid crowd was eighth of ten on FutureX-Past.
agent_relevance: Twenty-five votes from similar models count as a few. If an agent has several samplers, group them by behaviour and count one vote per group (G4).

source: Chetlapalli, Liao, Chen, Chen (2026) Diverse by Reasoning: Harnessing the Wisdom of LLM Crowds for Future Prediction (table and random controls)
finding: Medoid crowd: FutureX-Past 0.302, BTF-v3 0.810. All-model voting 0.296 and 0.800. Performance-based expert 0.265 and 0.790. Picking the most mutually different models did worse than random.
numbers: K-means++ medoid line-up at the 88th percentile of 1000 random one-per-cluster line-ups on BTF-v3 (829 worse, 92 identical, 79 better) and the 83rd on FutureX-Past. k=4 most-dissimilar voting at the 5th percentile on FutureX-Past (worse than 947 of 1000 random). Committee size alone correlates +0.505 with score; at fixed size internal disagreement correlates +0.211, positive in all 7 size strata.
limits: Random line-ups match the medoid crowd in about one draw in eight, so the effect is real but modest. Cluster subcommittee voting did not beat all-model voting.
agent_relevance: Maximum diversity is not the goal. Diversity of error without individual competence adds noise. Page's theorem needs both. No persona or strategy voters on single-answer problems (G4) fits.

source: Abels and Lenaerts (2025) Wisdom from Diversity: Bias Mitigation Through Hybrid Human-LLM Crowds
finding: Averaging many LLMs can amplify bias, because LLM errors are highly correlated. Humans are individually worse but far more diverse. Mixed human-LLM crowds beat both pure groups.
numbers: 18 LLMs vs a human dataset on bias-eliciting headlines. LLMs show much higher pairwise Q-statistic (error association) than humans. LLM group accuracy flattens as group size grows; human groups keep gaining; hybrid ensembles gain up to group size 4, then effects cancel.
limits: Narrow task (headline likelihood ratings). Needs human data.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that independence is the limiting condition for LLM crowds. More samples from the same family give diminishing returns (G4).

source: Abels and Lenaerts (2025) Wisdom from Diversity: Bias Mitigation Through Hybrid Human-LLM Crowds (weighted aggregation)
finding: Locally weighted aggregation (ExpertiseTree) beat simple averaging for hybrid groups. Plain averaging was the worst way to use correlated voters.
numbers: Across six headline categories: simple average of hybrid crowd about 0.50-0.80 accuracy; ExpertiseTree on hybrid about 0.73-0.83; on hybrid+ (top-MMLU LLMs plus random humans) about 0.75-0.89.
limits: Weights need labelled history. Table values read from extracted text.
agent_relevance: Weights need outcome history. Without it, code-based checks (G3) are the substitute.

source: The Wisdom of Artificial Deliberative Crowds (2026)
finding: Models from three families in small deliberating groups that reach consensus beat passive averaging of independent answers across four tasks. The gain disappeared when the group was clones of one model.
numbers: Four studies: visual numerosity estimation, peer review of 100 NeurIPS 2024 submissions, detecting hidden malicious agent behaviour, sports forecasting vs a prediction market. Clone groups showed no benefit.
limits: Cuts against much of the debate literature below. Needs mixed families and a fixed three-stage protocol (individual, group consensus, individual again).
agent_relevance: Deliberation helps only with diverse participants. That supports the bar in G9: single-model debate has no independence to exploit.

source: The Wisdom of Artificial Deliberative Crowds (2026) (clone test)
finding: Heterogeneous groups improved, same-model groups did not, matched on protocol, task and agent count.
numbers: Study 1 homogeneous groups: Anthropic z=1.22 p=0.22 d=0.087; OpenAI z=0.51 p=0.61 d=0.144; Google z=0.30 p=0.76 d=0.062. A later study: heterogeneous z=2.27 p=0.023 d=0.26; homogeneous Anthropic p=0.098 d=0.10, OpenAI p=0.87, Google p=0.64. Bayes factors about 5 to 12 for the null in clone groups.
limits: Small effects. Three families only.
agent_relevance: A clean causal test that diversity is the active ingredient.

source: The Wisdom of Artificial Deliberative Crowds (2026) (market comparison)
finding: Deliberated forecasts did better than independent averaging against a real betting market, and came close to the market.
numbers: Deliberation vs independent aggregation: Wilcoxon z=3.16, p=0.0016, paired d=0.49. In one comparison the deliberated group was indistinguishable from the market (z=0.48, p=0.63, BF 6.03 for null).
limits: Sports events only. Result is parity with the market, not superiority.
agent_relevance: Aggregation of diverse models can approach, not exceed, a good market.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models
finding: Different LLMs make the same wrong choices far more often than chance. Bigger, more accurate models are more alike in their mistakes.
numbers: 349 LLMs on 12,032 multiple-choice questions (HF leaderboard); 71 LLMs on 14,042 (HELM); 20 LLMs on 1,800 resume-job pairs. Pairs agree about 60% of the time when both are wrong (HELM). Some pairs reach 0.97 agreement when both wrong.
limits: Multiple-choice format makes agreement easier. Correlation rises with shared provider, architecture and size.
agent_relevance: The core threat to G4: as models improve, vote independence falls. Even different vendors do not give independent errors.

source: Kim, Garg, Peng, Garg (2025) Correlated Errors in Large Language Models (judges and hiring)
finding: A model judge inflates scores of models similar to itself, especially from the same provider. Using the same LLM for screening raised systemic exclusion in a hiring simulation.
numbers: Judge accuracy inflation measured against ground truth on leaderboard data; inflation larger for same-family and less accurate models.
limits: Observational on public leaderboards.
agent_relevance: Supports G5: never let a model from the same family judge candidates, and keep judging in code.

source: Kohli (2026) Nine Judges, Two Effective Votes
finding: A panel of 9 frontier LLM judges from 7 families carried the information of about 2 independent votes.
numbers: 1,000 items over MNLI, SNLI, AlphaNLI (100 human annotations each). Kish n_eff 2.18 (95% CI 2.07-2.31). Independence ratio 0.391. 290 items had 0 judges wrong and 51 had all 9 wrong (under 1 expected if independent). Permutation p<1e-4.
limits: NLI labels only. Human annotator disagreement sets the ceiling.
agent_relevance: A concrete formula to count real voters: n_eff. Nine samples worth two is a usable rule of thumb for G4.

source: Kohli (2026) Nine Judges, Two Effective Votes (panel vs best judge)
finding: The panel did not beat its best member, and smarter aggregation did not help.
numbers: MNLI: panel 72.0% vs best judge Qwen3-32B 71.8% (+0.2pp). SNLI: best judge Claude Sonnet 4.5 84.2% vs panel 77.7%. AlphaNLI: best 91.2% vs panel 88.7%. Established aggregation methods closed at most 11% of the gap to independent voting, even with access to correct answers.
limits: Three NLI tasks, one prompt design.
agent_relevance: Vote only when voters are known to be independent; otherwise prefer the best single procedure plus a check.

source: Lefort et al. (2024) Examining Independence in Ensemble Sentiment Analysis: Condorcet Jury Theorem
finding: Majority voting over sentiment classifiers including GPT-4 gave only marginal gains. The authors tie this to a lack of independence between the models.
numbers: Bagging and majority-vote variants differed from the best single model by about 0.00 to 0.01 in accuracy (Table 5). Three-class task; random baseline 0.33.
limits: Financial sentiment only. The authors extend the theorem to multi-class themselves.
agent_relevance: A failed-replication data point: Condorcet gains vanish when errors are shared.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Self-Consistency Improves Chain of Thought Reasoning in Language Models
finding: Sampling many reasoning paths from one model and taking the most common final answer raises accuracy, even though the samples are not independent.
numbers: PaLM-540B GSM8K 56.5 to 74.4 (+17.9 points). Also SVAMP +11.0, AQuA +12.2, StrategyQA +6.4, ARC-challenge +3.9 (abstract).
limits: It works because wrong paths scatter while right ones agree; it needs answers that can be compared exactly. No independence guarantee.
agent_relevance: This is the cheap single-model vote that G4 allows as a hint. It works when wrong answers are spread out, not when the model has one favoured error.

source: Huang et al. (2023) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet
finding: Debate between copies of one model is no better than self-consistency at an equal number of responses.
numbers: GSM8K with 6 responses: multi-agent debate round 2 83.2%, self-consistency 85.3%.
limits: One model family; GSM8K for this comparison.
agent_relevance: Supports G9: pay for samples and a vote, not for talk.

source: Debate or Vote authors (2025) Debate or Vote: Which Yields Better Decisions in Multi-Agent LLMs
finding: Majority voting accounts for most of the gains credited to multi-agent debate. Theory: debate makes each agent's belief a martingale, so it does not move expected correctness.
numbers: Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct, mean accuracy over 7 benchmarks: single agent 0.7205; majority voting 0.7691; decentralized debate T=2 0.7377, T=3 0.7112, T=5 0.7050; sparse T=2 0.7330; centralized T=2 0.6551. Arithmetic: single 0.814, voting 0.990, centralized debate 0.43-0.55.
limits: Small open models. The authors show modified debate that biases the martingale can help.
agent_relevance: Strong support for no debate (G9) and for voting only as a hint. Voting itself relies on diverse samples.

source: Wynn, Satija, Hadfield (2025) Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate
finding: Debate among models of different strength can lower accuracy. Models often flip from right to wrong to agree with peers, even when stronger models are the majority.
numbers: Accuracy drops across debate rounds in many group set-ups; flip-to-incorrect rates analysed (Figure 4). Exact percentages not extracted.
limits: Exact numbers not extracted. Task set limited.
agent_relevance: Conformity pressure inside LLM groups: a vote taken after exchange is no longer independent (G4, G9).

source: Wang et al. (2024) Mixture-of-Agents Enhances Large Language Model Capabilities
finding: Layered system where each model reads the previous layer's answers and rewrites. An open-source-only mix beat GPT-4o on AlpacaEval 2.0.
numbers: AlpacaEval 2.0 win rate 65.1% vs GPT-4 Omni 57.5% (+7.6 absolute). MoA-Lite 59.3%. The text also gives 65.8% in one place. Heterogeneous proposers contributed more than the same model repeated (Sec 3.3).
limits: Judged by an LLM judge, so verbosity and self-preference bias are possible. Agents read each other's output so answers are not independent by design.
agent_relevance: Model diversity helps generation. The aggregator is another model, which G5 would not allow without checks.

source: Talebirad et al. (2026) Wisdom of the Machines: Exploring Collective Intelligence in LLM Crowds (AAMAS)
finding: Temperature sampling from one model gave no significant benefit over a diverse set of models at temperature 0. Median of deterministic multi-model outputs was the best strategy.
numbers: Three vision-estimation datasets (height-weight pairs, small objects with known weight, Amazon prices); temperatures 0.2 to 1.0. Median of deterministic multi-model answers beat 68% of individual guesses on average; Amazon price mean relative error fell from 88% to 45% (p=0.025) in one comparison.
limits: Numeric estimation from images, not reasoning problems. Some statistics read from table text only.
agent_relevance: Direct test of sampling one model at high temperature versus using different models: model diversity wins, and temperature diversity costs more tokens for nothing here.

source: Verga et al. (2024) Replacing Judges with Juries: Evaluating LLM Generations with a Panel of Diverse Models
finding: A panel of three smaller models from different families judged generations better than one large judge and cost far less, and cut self-preference.
numbers: Panel: Command R, Haiku, GPT-3.5. Kappa 0.763 (NQ), 0.906 (TriviaQA), 0.867 (HotpotQA) and 7 to 8 times lower cost than GPT-4, both from a secondary summary, not checked.
limits: Not opened by me. Kohli (2026) finds panel gains can be near zero when judges are correlated.
agent_relevance: Diverse small judges can be cheaper than one big one, but only if the families differ.

source: Douven (2026) note on the Schoenegger median aggregator
finding: Douven used the same median aggregator as Schoenegger on his own clean subset and still found the LLM crowd below the prediction market.
numbers: Median aggregator Brier 0.343 on the 94-item clean subset. Crowd still less accurate than the market at each model's training cutoff.
limits: Different questions from Schoenegger; not a direct rerun.
agent_relevance: Treat positive LLM-crowd results with suspicion unless the questions postdate training.
